newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: INDIGENOUS LEADER SATISFIED WITH NATIVE TITLE TALKS
The chairman of the Northern Land Council, Gallarwuy Yunupingu says he's looking forward to thrashing out the Native Title issue with the Government and pastoralists.
This follows yesterday's meeting betweeen the Prime Minister and Indigenous leaders in Canberra about the issue.
Mr Yunupingu says John Howard has agreed to bring parties together to address issues arising from the High Court ruling that native title and pastoral leases can co-exist.
He says all delegates were satisfied with Mr Howard's response.
Mr Yunipingu says meeting dates are yet to be set, and it's now up to those with the technical expertise to advise the Prime Minister.
VICTORIANS WARNED AS TEMPERATURES SET TO SOAR
Victorians are being warned they could die of heatstroke, as high temperatures continue around the state, with 37-degrees predicted today.
The chief health officer Doctor Graham Rouch says elderly people and the very young are most at risk, but heatstroke can affect anyone exposed to excessive hot weather.
Ambulance officers say there were 13 cases of heatstroke yesterday, and many other incidents caused by the heat -- when the temperature reached 37 degrees.
They're expecting a similar number of incidents today.
WHITLAM LECTURE SERIES
ACTU President Jennie George says a new annual lecture series named after former Prime Minister Gough Whitlam, will be important in guiding social democratic debate.
Mr Whitlam will deliver the first of the lectures at the Sydney Town Hall on Sunday; other lecturers include Aboriginal advocate Noel Pearson and former New South Wales Premier Neville Wran.
The Union movment says the series aims to counter the conservative ideology being put forward in public debate.
Ms George says the idea of the series is to build on the foundations of broadly social democratic values.
The launch will also see the announcement of a new foundation to improve training for union representatives.
ASHBURTON RIVER PEAKS
In Western Australia's Pilbara, the State Emergency Service says an aerial check at first light will determine the river height of the Ashburton River.
The River is peaking as it passes through the Nanutarra Bridge.
S-E-S Regional Manager, Dennis Rayner, says the mass of water is about 12 kilometres long and five kilometres wide.
Fifteen people have been evacuated from the Nanutarra Roadhouse, 13-hundred kilometres north of Perth, and the Nanutarra Homestead has flooded for the first time in its 110 year history.
He says at last report about six o'closk last night, the Homestead had about a metre of water passing through it.
WILLIAMS CALLS ON STATES TO STICK TO LEGAL AID SYSTEM
Federal Attorney General, Daryl Williams, has called on the States to stick with the present system of co-operative agreements, as the best way to deliver legal aid.
Some States and Territories have threatened to break away because the Federal Government cut 120 million dollars over three years rom legal aid in its August budget.
The States say the cuts are unfair and will leave people unrepresented, possibly meaning trials are called off because the accused can't afford a lawyer.
But Mr Williams says the States should pay for representation for people charged under State laws.
He says he'll keep working to continue the co-operative system with the States.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
